episodes.title: Hello and Welcome
episodes.summary: Sam and Alex say hello and talk about where they are from and what they do.
lines: Hello and welcome to the WordCards Podcast! My name is Sam.
And I'm Alex. Hi, everyone!
This is a podcast for English learners. We speak slowly and we use easy words.
That's right. Today we want to say hello and tell you about us.
Alex, where are you from?
I'm from Canada. I live in a small city near the sea. And you, Sam?
I'm from England, but now I live in Istanbul.
Istanbul! That's a big city.
Yes, it's very big. And it's very beautiful.
Do you speak Turkish?
A little. I can say "merhaba" and "teşekkürler". That means "hello" and "thank you".
Very good! I can't speak Turkish, but I want to learn.
What do you do, Alex?
I'm a teacher. I teach music to children.
Do you play an instrument?
Yes, I play the guitar and the piano. What about you?
I don't play an instrument. I'm a cook. I work in a restaurant.
Oh, I love food! What is your favourite food?
My favourite food is soup. I make soup every day.
Every day? Wow!
Well, that's all for today. Thank you for listening!
See you next time. Bye!

questions.q: Where is Alex from?
Where does Sam live now?
options: In a small city near the sea

questions.q: What is Alex's job?
What is Sam's favourite food?

episodes.title: A Day in My Life
episodes.summary: What time do you get up? Sam and Alex talk about their daily routines.
lines: Hi, I'm Alex.
And I'm Sam. Welcome to the WordCards Podcast.
Today our topic is daily routines. What do you do every day?
Let's start in the morning. Alex, what time do you get up?
I get up at half past six. It's very early, I know.
That is early! I get up at eight o'clock.
After I get up, I take a shower and I drink a cup of coffee.
Do you eat breakfast?
Yes, I always eat breakfast. I usually have bread, cheese and an egg.
I never eat breakfast. I'm not hungry in the morning.
Really? How do you go to work?
I walk to work. The restaurant is near my home. It takes ten minutes.
I go to school by bus. It takes thirty minutes.
What do you do in the evening?
I cook dinner, and then I read a book or watch TV.
I work in the evening. The restaurant is very busy at night.
So when do you finish work?
At eleven o'clock. Then I go home and sleep.
And I go to bed at ten. We have very different days!
Yes, we do. Now it's your turn. What time do you get up? Say it in English!
Thanks for listening. Bye!

questions.q: What time does Alex get up?
What does Sam eat for breakfast?
How does Alex go to school?
When does Sam finish work?

episodes.title: At the Café
episodes.summary: Sam is the waiter and Alex is the customer. Learn how to order food and drinks.
lines: Hello, and welcome to the WordCards Podcast. Today we are at a café!
Well, not really. We are in our studio. But let's play a game.
OK. I'm the waiter, and you are the customer. Ready?
Ready!
Good afternoon. Can I help you?
Yes, please. Can I have a tea, please?
Of course. Black tea or green tea?
Black tea, please. With milk.
And sugar?
No sugar, thank you.
Would you like something to eat?
Hmm. What do you have?
We have chocolate cake, apple cake and sandwiches.
How much is the apple cake?
It's four euros.
OK, one apple cake, please.
Here you are. One black tea with milk and one apple cake.
Thank you. Can I pay by card?
Yes, of course. That's six euros, please.
Here you are.
Thank you. Have a nice day!
You too! That was fun, Sam.
Yes! Remember these questions: "Can I have a tea, please?" and "How much is the cake?"
Try them at your next café. Bye for now!

questions.q: What does Alex drink?
Does Alex want sugar?
How much is the apple cake?
How does Alex pay?

episodes.title: Weekend Plans
episodes.summary: It's Friday! Sam and Alex talk about their plans for the weekend and how to talk about the future.
lines: Hi everyone, and welcome back to the WordCards Podcast. I'm Sam.
And I'm Alex. It's Friday today, so we're talking about the weekend.
I love Fridays. Alex, what are you going to do this weekend?
On Saturday morning, I'm going to visit my grandmother. She lives in a village about an hour from the city.
That's nice. How often do you see her?
Once a month. She always cooks a huge lunch, so I never eat breakfast before I go!
Good idea. What about Saturday evening?
Some friends are coming to my flat. We're going to play board games.
Board games? Which ones?
Usually card games, or a game about building cities. Sometimes it takes three hours to finish!
Three hours! I can't sit still for that long.
What about you, Sam? Are you working this weekend?
I'm working on Saturday, but Sunday is my day off. If the weather is good, I'm going to go cycling by the sea.
And if it rains?
Then I'm going to stay at home, clean my flat and watch a film. Not very exciting, but relaxing.
Sometimes a quiet weekend is the best weekend.
I agree. Last weekend I went to a concert, and I got home at two in the morning. I was so tired on Monday.
Who did you see?
A jazz band from Brazil. They were amazing.
Here's a tip for our listeners: when you talk about your plans, use "going to". For example, "I'm going to visit my grandmother."
And when you make plans with other people, you can also use the present continuous: "Some friends are coming to my flat."
So, what are you going to do this weekend? Tell a friend in English!
Have a great weekend, everyone!

questions.q: Who is Alex going to visit on Saturday morning?
Why doesn't Alex eat breakfast before the visit?
options: Because their grandmother cooks a big lunch
Because there is no food at home

questions.q: What is Sam going to do on Sunday if it rains?
options: Clean the flat and watch a film

questions.q: What did Sam do last weekend?

episodes.title: A Train Journey
episodes.summary: Alex travelled to the mountains by train. Not everything went well, but the trip was still great.
lines: Welcome to the WordCards Podcast. Alex, you went on holiday last month, didn't you?
Yes, I did. I went to the mountains for a week, and I travelled by train.
Why the train? Flying is faster.
That's true, but from a train you can see the country. And it's better for the environment.
How long was the journey?
About nine hours. I had to change trains twice.
Nine hours! Weren't you bored?
Not at all. I read a book, listened to music and looked out of the window. The views were beautiful: lakes, forests, small villages.
Did everything go well?
Well, not everything. My first train was late, so I missed the next one.
Oh no! What did you do?
I went to the ticket office and asked for help. The man there was very kind. He changed my ticket, and I took the next train an hour later.
Did you have to pay again?
No, it was free, because the first train was late.
That's lucky. And what did you do in the mountains?
I walked a lot. Every morning I went for a long walk, and in the afternoon I sat in a café and wrote postcards.
Postcards? Does anyone still send postcards?
I do! My grandmother loves them.
Here are some useful questions for train travel: "Can I have a return ticket, please?", "Which platform does the train leave from?" and "Is this seat free?"
Good ones. Next time you travel, try them!
Thanks for listening. See you soon!

questions.q: How long was Alex's train journey?
Why did Alex miss a train?
How much did the new ticket cost?
What did Alex do in the afternoons?

episodes.title: Starting a New Hobby
episodes.summary: Sam started growing vegetables on a small balcony. How did it start, and what went wrong?
lines: Hello and welcome to the WordCards Podcast. Today's topic is hobbies.
And Sam has a new hobby, right?
Yes! Three months ago, I started growing vegetables on my balcony.
On a balcony? Is there enough space?
It's a small balcony, but you don't need much space. I have tomatoes, peppers and some herbs, like mint and basil.
Why did you start?
I wanted to spend less time on my phone. After work, I was always looking at a screen. Now I go outside, water my plants and relax.
Was it difficult at the beginning?
Yes, a bit. My first tomatoes died because I gave them too much water.
Oh no!
So I watched some videos and asked my neighbour for advice. She has a beautiful garden. Now I water the plants every two days, not every day.
And have you eaten any of your vegetables yet?
Yes! Last week I made a salad with my own tomatoes. It was the best salad of my life.
I'm sure it was. I'd like a new hobby too, but I never have time.
You don't need a lot of time. Fifteen minutes a day is enough for many hobbies.
That's true. Maybe I'll try drawing. I liked it when I was a child.
Great idea! You only need a pencil and some paper.
Here's a question for you, listeners: do you have a hobby? When did you start it?
Answer in English, out loud or in a notebook. Thanks for listening!

questions.q: What does Sam grow on the balcony?
Why did Sam start this hobby?
options: To spend less time on the phone

questions.q: Why did the first tomatoes die?
What hobby does Alex want to try?

episodes.title: Why We Forget New Words
episodes.summary: Why do we forget words so quickly, and what can we do about it? The science behind spaced repetition.
lines: Welcome to the WordCards Podcast. Today we're talking about something every language learner knows well: forgetting.
Oh yes. I learn ten new words on Monday, and by Friday I remember maybe two.
You're not alone. In the 1880s, a German scientist called Hermann Ebbinghaus studied his own memory. He learned lists of nonsense words and tested himself again and again.
Nonsense words? Why not real ones?
Because he didn't want his knowledge of real words to help him. He wanted to measure memory itself.
Clever. So what did he find?

He found that we forget very quickly at first. Within a day, a large part of what we learned is gone. After that, forgetting slows down. He drew it as a line on a graph, and today we call it the forgetting curve.
That sounds a bit depressing.
But there's good news. Ebbinghaus also noticed that every time he reviewed the words, he forgot them more slowly. So each review makes the memory stronger.
So the answer is to repeat the words many times?
Yes, but the timing matters. If you review a word five times in one evening, it doesn't help much. It's much better to review it after one day, then after a few days, and then after a week or two.
That's called spaced repetition, isn't it? It's how the flashcards in this app work.
Exactly. A card that you know comes back later and later. A card that you forget comes back soon.
Are there any other tips?
A few. First, try to remember the word before you look at the answer. That small effort is what builds the memory.
So it's good if it feels a little difficult.
Right. Second, learn words in context, in a sentence or a story, not on their own.
Like listening to a podcast!
Ha, yes. And third, sleep well. Your brain organises new memories while you sleep.
So I should study a little every day, test myself, and go to bed on time.
That's the summary. Even ten minutes a day is better than two hours once a week.
OK, listeners, here's your homework: go and review your cards today!
Thanks for listening, and see you next time.

questions.q: Why did Ebbinghaus use nonsense words?
options: So that his knowledge of real words would not help him

questions.q: When do we forget the fastest?
Which way of reviewing works best?
options: After a day, then after a few days, then after a week

questions.q: Which tip is NOT in the episode?
options: Try to remember the word before you look at the answer
Study for two hours once a week
Learn words in a sentence or a story

episodes.title: Why Sleep Matters
episodes.summary: Alex stayed up late watching a series. Sam explains what happens when we don't sleep enough.
lines: Hello and welcome to the WordCards Podcast. Alex, you look tired today.
I am. I went to bed after one o'clock last night. I was watching a series and I couldn't stop.
"Just one more episode." We've all done that. Actually, that's our topic today: sleep.
Good, I need this one. So how much sleep do adults need?
Most experts say between seven and nine hours a night. Teenagers need even more.
I don't think I've slept nine hours since I was a child.
Lots of people haven't. But sleep isn't just rest. While we sleep, the brain is very busy. It sorts through the day and stores important memories.
So if I sleep badly, I learn less?
That's what research suggests. People who sleep well after learning something usually remember it better the next day.
And what happens when we don't get enough sleep?
In the short term, it's harder to concentrate, and we're more likely to make mistakes. We also feel hungrier and more emotional.
That explains why I wanted chocolate all morning.
Exactly! And over many years, poor sleep is also connected to health problems, like heart disease.
OK, I'm convinced. How can I sleep better?
There are a few simple things. Go to bed and get up at the same time every day, even at weekends.
Even at weekends? That's hard.
It is, but it helps your body clock. Also, keep your bedroom dark and cool, and avoid coffee in the afternoon.
And what about phones?
Try to put your phone away about an hour before bed. Both the light from the screen and the things you read keep your brain awake.
So, no series after midnight.
Maybe watch the next episode tomorrow. It will still be there.
Good advice. Listeners, how many hours did you sleep last night? Thanks for listening!

questions.q: How much sleep do most adults need?
What does the brain do while we sleep?
options: It sorts through the day and stores memories

questions.q: Which is a short-term effect of not sleeping enough?
What does Sam say about phones?
options: Use your phone in bed to relax
Only use it to listen to music
Put it away about an hour before bed

episodes.title: The True Cost of Cheap Clothes
episodes.summary: Fast fashion is cheap in the shop, but who pays the real price? Sam and Alex discuss the environment, workers and our wardrobes.
lines: Welcome to the WordCards Podcast. Sam, how many items of clothing have you bought this year?
Honestly? I'd rather not count. Quite a few, probably. Why?
Because today we're discussing fast fashion: cheap, trendy clothes that are produced quickly and in huge quantities.
The kind of shop where the whole collection seems to change every couple of weeks.
Exactly. A few decades ago, most brands released new collections a few times a year, roughly one per season. Now some of them add new designs almost every day.
And the prices are incredibly low. A T-shirt can cost less than a sandwich.

That's the point. The price on the label doesn't include the real cost. Take cotton, for example. It needs an enormous amount of water. One widely quoted estimate is that a single cotton T-shirt takes around two thousand seven hundred litres of water to make.
That's more than one person drinks in a couple of years.
Then there are synthetic fabrics like polyester, which are made from oil. Every time you wash them, tiny plastic fibres end up in rivers and the sea.
And what about the people who make the clothes? That's the part we usually don't see.

Right. Many garment workers earn very low wages and work long hours, sometimes in unsafe buildings. In 2013, a factory building called Rana Plaza collapsed in Bangladesh, and more than a thousand workers died.
I remember that. It was a turning point for a lot of people.
It was. But the deeper problem is how we treat clothes. Many items are worn only a handful of times before they're thrown away.
OK, but let's be fair. Not everyone can afford expensive, ethical brands. Cheap clothing really matters to people on low incomes.
That's an important point, and this isn't about making anyone feel guilty. In fact, the most sustainable option is often the cheapest one: buying less and wearing what we already have for longer.
So repairing things, buying second-hand, swapping clothes with friends.
Exactly. One useful question to ask yourself before you buy something is: "Will I wear this at least thirty times?"
Thirty times. That would rule out half of my wardrobe.
Mine too, to be honest. So, listeners, have a look in your wardrobe this week. Which item have you worn the most, and which have you never worn at all?
Thanks for listening, and see you next time.

questions.q: What is "fast fashion"?
options: Expensive clothes that last a long time
Cheap, trendy clothes made quickly and in large amounts

questions.q: What problem with polyester is mentioned?
options: Washing it releases tiny plastic fibres into rivers and the sea
It needs a lot of water to grow

questions.q: What point does Sam make in defence of cheap clothes?
options: They are better for the environment
People on low incomes need affordable clothing

questions.q: What question does Alex suggest asking before buying something?
options: Will I wear this at least thirty times?

episodes.title: Working From Home: Dream or Trap?
episodes.summary: No commute and more freedom, but also loneliness and longer hours. Is working from home really better?
lines: Hello and welcome to the WordCards Podcast. Alex, as a teacher you can't really work from home, can you?
Not the teaching itself, no. But I do a lot of my planning and marking at home. And during the pandemic, I taught online for months.
How was that?
Exhausting, honestly. Teaching music through a laptop camera is far from ideal. But for many office workers, that period changed everything.
Right. Before 2020, working from home was a rare privilege. Then, almost overnight, millions of people were doing it.
And plenty of them never went back full-time. Lots of companies now offer hybrid work: a few days in the office and a few days at home.
So what are the advantages? The obvious one is no commute.
That's huge. If you spend an hour travelling each way, working from home gives you back ten hours a week. People use that time to sleep, exercise or be with their families.
There's flexibility, too. You can put the washing on between meetings or take your kids to school.
And some people find they concentrate better without the noise and interruptions of an open-plan office.
But I imagine there are downsides.
Definitely. The biggest one for many people is loneliness. You lose those casual conversations by the coffee machine.
And those conversations matter more than we think. That's often how people share ideas, or learn from more experienced colleagues.
Yes, especially young employees. It's hard to learn a job when you never see how other people do it.
Another problem is that the line between work and home becomes blurred. When your office is your kitchen table, when does the working day actually end?
That's the trap. Some people end up working longer hours than before, answering emails late at night.
So, what's the solution?

Boundaries. Have a fixed finishing time, a separate place to work if you can, and turn off notifications in the evening. Some people even take a short walk at the end of the day, as a kind of fake commute.
A fake commute! I like that.
And on office days, make the most of being together: meetings, teamwork, lunch with colleagues. Save the work that needs deep focus for home.
So the answer isn't home or office, but using each one for what it's good at.
Exactly. Listeners, which would you choose, and why? Thanks for listening!

questions.q: What is "hybrid work"?
options: Working two jobs at the same time
Some days in the office and some days at home

questions.q: How much time can someone with a one-hour commute each way save?
Why is working from home especially hard for young employees?
options: It is harder to learn by watching colleagues
They have less space at home

questions.q: What is a "fake commute"?
options: Pretending to be in the office
A short walk at the end of the working day
Driving to a café to work
